rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people meant by al-nās are Muhammad’s Companions and those who believed in him; the definite article points to people already known to the addressees.
rows.anchor: المراد بالناس في هذه الآية أصحاب محمد - صلى الله عليه وسلم - والذين آمنوا به، في قول الجميع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question in anūʾminu is a denial: they reject imitating the believers.
rows.anchor: استفهام [معناه: الجحد والإنكار (¬4)، لا نفعل كما فعلوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-sufahāʾ are ignorant people with deficient intellect; the source explains safah as lightness and cites light-minded usage for winds and a camel.
rows.anchor: والسفهاء: الجهال (¬6) الذين قلت عقولهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For this reason God calls children and women fools in 4:5; the hypocrites also use al-sufahāʾ for Muhammad’s Companions, with the same definite article as al-nās.
rows.anchor: ولهذا المعنى سمى الله تعالى الصبيان والنساء: السفهاء في قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hypocrites voiced their claim that believers were fools among themselves, not in front of believers, as 2:14 shows.
rows.anchor: قيل: إنهم كانوا يظهرون هذا القول فيما بينهم، لا عند المؤمنين؛

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The believers whom the hypocrites meet are identified as Abū Bakr and his companions.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون: يعني: أبا بكر -رضي الله عنه- وأصحابه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The form laqū comes from laqiyū; a heavy yāʾ was dropped and its ḍamma transferred to the preceding qāf.
rows.anchor: و (لقوا) في الأصل (لقيوا) فاستثقلت الضمة على # (الياء)، فحذفت

rows.speaker: الحراني عن ابن السكيت
rows.claim: Ibn al-Sikkīt lists the forms liqāʾ, liqyān, liqyā, and laqā for meeting.
rows.anchor:
الحراني عن ابن السكيت:
لقيته لقاء ولقيانا ولقيا

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Al-Layth says a thing is met when it faces or encounters another thing.
rows.anchor: الليث: وكل شيء استقبل شيئا أو صادفه فقد لقيه

rows.speaker: النضر
rows.claim: Al-Nadr takes ilā in khalaw ilā as maʿa and cites parallels in 2:187, 3:52 and 61:14, and 4:2.
rows.anchor: وقال النضر (¬2): (إلى) هاهنا بمعنى: (مع) (¬3)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The grammarians understand the hypocrites as leaving believers and going to their chiefs; the author prefers the ordinary endpoint sense of ilā over treating it as maʿa.
rows.anchor: وهذا أحسن من إخراج # (إلى) عن حدها (¬1)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A shayṭān is any rebellious, defiant being among jinn or humans, as 6:112 calls human and jinn tempters shayāṭīn.
rows.anchor: والشيطان كل متمرد عات من الجن والإنس (¬2)

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Al-Layth derives shayṭān as fayʿāl from shatana, to be distant; he also connects shayṭana with becoming and acting like Satan.
rows.anchor: فقال الليث: الشيطان فيعال من شطن أي: بعد

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some derive shayṭān as faʿlān from shāṭa, to perish or burn; al-Aʿshā’s verse yushīṭ is cited as evidence.
rows.anchor: وقال قوم: الشيطان فعلان من شاط يشيط إذا هلك واحترق

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī argues shayṭān is fayʿāl from shatana, not faʿlān from yashīṭ; the following segment gives his morphological evidence.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي: هو (فيعال) من شطن (¬5) مثل: البيطار والغيداق

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī rejects faʿlān because Sibawayh attests shayṭana on the fayʿal pattern; Amiyya’s shāṭin likewise has n as the root’s final radical, establishing shayṭān as fayʿāl.
rows.anchor: لأن سيبويه قد حكى: (شيطن) (¬1) وهو (فيعل) لا (فعلن)،

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Amiyya’s line is decisive: shāṭin is an active participle with n as its final root consonant, so shayṭān is fayʿāl and not faʿlān from yashīṭ.
rows.anchor: فكما أن (شاطنا) فاعل، والنون لام، كذلك (شيطان) فيعال

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq explains shayṭān as one extreme in unbelief and far removed from the truth, among jinn or humans.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: ومعنى الشيطان: الغالي في الكفر المتبعد فيه من الجن والإنس

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the hypocrites’ shayāṭīn are their chiefs and leaders.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: أراد بشياطينهم كبراءهم وقادتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maʿa joins one thing to another and is accusative like an adverb because ana maʿaka means I am settled with you.
rows.anchor: (مع) كلمة تضم الشيء إلى الشيء، ونصبها كنصب الظروف؛

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Huzʾ means ridicule: the mocker outwardly shows something other than what is inward, to belittle and play around.
rows.anchor: وهو أن يظهر غير ما يضمر استصغارا وعبثا (¬6)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Purchase means exchange, but not every exchange is a purchase; using the purchase metaphor stresses eagerness, since the buyer wants what he takes and Arabic calls preference a sale even without an actual transaction.
rows.anchor: حقيقة الاشتراء: الاستبدال، وكل اشتراء استبدال، وليس كل استبدال اشتراء،

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses the transaction as taking misguidance and leaving guidance.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس في هذه الآية: أخذوا الضلالة وتركوا الهدى

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: Scholars of meaning say the hypocrites never possessed guidance; they abandoned its obligation and replaced it with misguidance, so the verse describes them as buying it.
rows.anchor: قال أهل المعاني: هؤلاء المنافقون لم يكونوا على الهدى قط،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ishtaraw derives from ishtariyū; vowel change and deletion leave the plural wāw beside the silent definite article, requiring a linking vowel.
rows.anchor: وأصل {اشتروا} اشتريوا، فلما تحركت (الياء) وانفتح ما قبلها صارت (ألفا)،

rows.speaker: أكثر النحويين
rows.claim: Most grammarians say plural wāws take ḍamma because it marks plurality; by contrast, nonplural wāws take kasra.
rows.anchor: فقال أكثر النحويين: إن واوات الجمع كلها (¬4) تحرك بالضم نحو: {لتبلون}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some grammarians permit kasra by analogy with law and aw law, and also permit ḍamma in law istataʿnā by analogy with the plural wāw.
rows.anchor: وقد أجازوا الكسر (¬1) في {اشتروا الضلالة} تشبيها بمثل: {لو استطعنا}

rows.speaker: ناس
rows.claim: Some say the wāw has ḍamma because it is semantically the subject; the author rejects this account, since an agentive yāʾ can take kasra and variants show the vowel is not inflection.
rows.anchor: فجعلت حركة التقاء الساكنين فيه كحركة الإعراب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because some read the wāw with kasra here and in 2:237, the proposal that its vowel is like inflection cannot explain the variation.
rows.anchor: وقوم كسروا الواو في مسألتنا (¬8) وفي قوله: {ولا تنسوا الفضل بينكم}

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says the wāw receives the ḍamma that would belong to the verb’s final radical.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: إنهم إنما حركوا (الواو) هاهنا بالحركة التي كانت تجب للام الفعل

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī rejects al-Farrāʾ’s account: vowel transfer moves to a preceding consonant, not a following one, as the cited forms show.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي (¬4): الذي ذهب إليه الفراء هو أن الحركة في (الواو)

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: If al-Farrāʾ were right, the wāw would move regardless of what follows; in fact it moves only when two silent letters meet, proving this vowel breaks a meeting of sukūns.
rows.anchor: فلما لم تتحرك الواو في {اشتروا} إلا عند التقاء ساكن، ثبت أن حركتها حركة الحروف الساكنة الملتقية

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq calls it mistaken to replace the wāw with hamza, since only a wāw whose ḍamma is fixed is hamzated; here the vowel is only for two adjacent sukūns.
rows.anchor: قال أبو أسحاق: من أبدل واو (¬3) {اشتروا الضلالة} همزة، غالط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ribḥ is increase over capital, and tijāra is circulating wealth to seek growth; a cited poem illustrates the verb tajara.
rows.anchor: (الربح) الزيادة على أصل المال (¬7). و (التجارة) تقليب الأموال وتصريفها لطلب النماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means they did not profit from their trade; Arabs attribute profit to a transaction, as in common expressions, 34:33, 47:21, and Jarīr’s poem attributing blindness and sight to night and day.
rows.anchor: ومعنى قوله {فما ربحت تجارتهم} أي ما ربحوا في تجارتهم، وأضاف الربح إلى التجارة

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ allows such attribution only when context makes the intended meaning clear; where ambiguous, a phrase like your servant lost could describe a trader or merchandise.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: وهذا إنما يجوز إذا عرف الكلام ولم يشكل، فإذا أشكل لم يجز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alladhīna describes al-fāsiqīn; naqḍ means undoing a firmly made rope or building, and poetic naqāʾiḍ are poems that answer and undo another poet’s poem, including those of Jarīr and al-Farazdaq.
rows.anchor: (والذين) من صفة الفاسقين. و (النقض) في # اللغة: الهدم، وإفساد ما أبرمته من حبل أو بناء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAhd here can mean a testament or command, as in 36:60, or the binding covenant that secures what follows.
rows.anchor: والذي أريد به هاهنا الوصية (¬10) والأمر من قولهم: عهد الخليفة إلى فلان

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq offers two covenants: the demand that prophets and followers not reject Muhammad, linked to 3:81, or the primordial covenant with Adam’s descendants in 7:172.
rows.anchor: أحدهما: ما أخذه على النبيين ومن اتبعهم ألا يكفروا بالنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prophetic covenant is stronger because God would not hold people to an unknown proof; the Adam covenant also holds because revelation made it known as if remembered.
rows.anchor: والوجه الأول أصحهما، من قبل أن الله لا يحتج عليهم بما لا يعرفون

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the covenant in 13:25 with God’s covenant in Adam’s loins, when the descendants answered that God is their Lord.
rows.anchor: وهذا (¬1) الوجه هو قول ابن عباس ذكره في قوله: {والذين ينقضون عهد الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mīm in min baʿdi is emphatic; mīthāq is what confirms something, and its yāʾ comes from wāw.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {من بعد ميثاقه}. (من) صلة لأجل التأكيد (¬4). والميثاق: ما وقع التوثيق

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ gives miyāthiq and mawāthiq as plurals of mīthāq and cites a verse using miyāthiq.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: يقال في جمع الميثاق: مياثق ومواثق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in mīthāq can refer to God, meaning God’s confirmation of the covenant, or to the covenant itself, meaning its confirmation and reinforcement.
rows.anchor: والكناية في الميثاق يجوز أن تكون (¬7) عائدة على الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation of severing what God ordered joined is severing kinship; Quraysh cut their relationship with the Prophet through hostility.
rows.anchor: يعني الأرحام (¬1)، وذلك أن قريشا قطعوا رحم النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم - بالمعاداة معه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another interpretation is rejecting some messengers and scriptures while accepting others, as in 4:150; Ibn ʿAbbās says believers join their belief by not distinguishing among God’s messengers.
rows.anchor: وهذا الوجه هو قول ابن عباس ذكره في الآية التي في (الرعد) (¬3)، وقال

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj parses an yūṣala as genitive apposition to the pronoun in mā, meaning what God commanded to be joined.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: وموضع {أن يوصل} خفض على، (¬5) البدل من (الهاء)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Corruption on earth means disobedience and obstructing people from believing in Muhammad.
rows.anchor: بالمعاصي، وتعويق الناس عن الإيمان بمحمد صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Losers first refers to losing capital in commerce; by extension these people lost the good they would have gained through faith, earned punishment, and missed reward.
rows.anchor: القوم نقصوا (¬4) بكفرهم راحة أنفسهم التي كانت لهم لو آمنوا

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq says inna is kasra because waṣṣā and awṣā mean speech: Abraham said that God had selected the religion for them.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: إنما كسرت (إن) لأن معنى وصى وأوصى: قول

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports Abraham telling his sons not to associate anything with God, even if they were sawn, cut with scissors, or burned.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: إن إبراهيم قال لبنيه: لا تعدلوا بالله شيئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The selected religion is Islam, the religion of ḥanīfiyya; its definite article is specific and referential, since Islam was selected over other religions, not the whole genus of religion.
rows.anchor: يريد: دين الإسلام دين الحنيفية، والألف واللام فيه للعهد لا للجنس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent command not to die is really a command not to abandon Islam, so that death will find them as Muslims; this is like telling someone not to let oneself see them here.
rows.anchor: ووقع النهي في ظاهر الكلام على الموت، وإنما نهوا في الحقيقة عن ترك الإسلام؛

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj paraphrases the command as remaining firmly Muslim, so that when death arrives it finds them in Islam.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: وهذا من سعة الكلام، والمعنى في الآية: ألزموا الإسلام

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ records the forms of māt: mawta, mayta, and mamāta, noting expressions for barren land, mass death, selling livestock versus other goods, and a person with a lifeless heart.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء في كتاب # المصادر: مات يموت موتا وميتة ومماتا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage was revealed concerning Jews who claimed Jacob had enjoined Judaism on his sons at his death.
rows.anchor: نزلت في اليهود حين قالوا للنبي صلى الله وسلم: ألست تعلم أن يعقوب يوم مات أوصى بنيه باليهودية؟

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq reads am as bal: the discourse turns from the previous point and asks whether they were witnesses.
rows.anchor: ومعناه: بل أكنتم، كأنه ترك الكلام الأول واستفهم، قاله أبو إسحاق (¬2).

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda takes am to mean hal, citing al-Akhṭal’s question about whether one saw Wāsiṭ.
rows.anchor: قاله أبو إسحاق (¬2). وقال أبو عبيدة:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively an initial question is understood: did the Jews learn what they attribute to Jacob, or were they present at his testament? The use of am was explained at 2:108.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يتقدمه استفهام مضمر، كأنه قيل لليهود: أبلغكم ما تقولون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shuhadāʾ means those present; idh is accusative as a time expression; the source also defines ḥuḍūr as opposite absence and ḥaḍrat as a man’s courtyard.
rows.anchor: الحضور خلاف الغيبة، وحضرة الرجل: فناؤه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second idh is accusative like the first and is an emphatic substitute for it.
rows.anchor: إذ هذه الثانية موضعها نصب، كموضع الأولى، وهو بدل مؤكد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ab has dialect forms abuka, abak, and abuk, with different duals and plurals; the source cites Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā and Sibawayh as poetic evidence.
rows.anchor: وفي الأب لغات، يقال: هذا أبك، وهذا أباك، وهذا أبوك

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Al-Layth says yaʾbū Tayman means to nourish him and taʾabbā so-and-so means to adopt him as a father; diminutives of abāʾ include abiyūn and abiyāʾ.
rows.anchor: الليث: فلان يأبو تيما إباوة بكسر الألف، أي: يغذوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ishmael is grouped with Jacob’s fathers although he was his uncle, because Arabs call an uncle a father.
rows.anchor: أدخله في جملة الأباء، وهو كان عم يعقوب؛ لأن العرب تسمي العم أبا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report about the conquest of Mecca has the Prophet call his uncle al-ʿAbbās his father and say an uncle is a counterpart of his father, confirming Arabic usage.
rows.anchor: يا عم، أما علمت أن عم الرجل صنو أبيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading has wa-ilāhi abīka Ibrāhīm; it may use plural abīn, or singular abīka may exclude Ishmael from the fathers and imply God of Abraham, Ishmael, and Isaac.
rows.anchor: أحدهما: أنه جمع الأب على أبين كما ذكرنا

rows.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report says every prophet was offered a choice between life and death; Jacob delayed his death to consult his twelve sons and their descendants, then asked whom they would worship.
rows.anchor: قال عطاء عن ابن عباس: إن الله لم يقبض نبيا حتى يخيره بين الموت والحياة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ilāhan wāḥidan can be circumstantial, worshipping God in a state of unity, or apposition, whose benefit is to state monotheism explicitly.
rows.anchor: ينتصب على وجهين: إن شئت على الحال، كأنهم قالوا: نعبد إلهك في حال وحدانية،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fa answers the preceding description: those who traded guidance for misguidance and forgiveness for punishment are, by implication, astonishingly patient toward the Fire.
rows.anchor: فأما المعنى: ففيه وجهان لأهل التأويل (¬1):

rows.speaker: أهل التأويل
rows.claim: One reported interpretation makes mā exclamatory; the author parses it as a subject, aḥsana as a past-tense verb and predicate, and Zaydan as its object.
rows.anchor: أحدهما: أن (ما) هاهنا تعجب (¬2)، كقولهم: ما أحسن زيدا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mā is chosen for exclamation because its ambiguity points to the surprising thing; shayʾ could imply belittling it or report a settled fact, whereas an exclamation startles the hearer.
rows.anchor: وخصت لفظة ما بالتعجب لإبهامها، وهي واقعة على الشيء الذي تتعجب منه،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Exclamative aḥsana is a triliteral verb shifted to a quadriliteral form; its fixed final fatḥa shows it is verbal, and the object is accusative because the thing is truly acted upon.
rows.anchor: فقد بان بما ذكرنا أن قوله: {فما أصبرهم} إذا # قلنا: إنه تعجب، فعل منقول من الثلاثي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The diminutive mā aḥaysana in poetry does not make the exclamative a noun; it only imitates nouns while remaining a verb.
rows.anchor: وتصغيره لا يدل على أنه اسم، وذلك أن فعل التعجب قد لزم طريقة واحدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ifrāgh literally means pouring and emptying a vessel; the prayer asks God to pour the fullest and most complete patience upon them.
rows.anchor: فمعنى {ربنا أفرغ علينا صبرا} أي: اصبب (¬5) علينا أتم صب وأبلغه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The request to steady their feet may mean strengthen their hearts, divide the enemy so they falter, cast fear into them so they show weakness, or provide any comparable cause of victory.
rows.anchor: {وثبت أقدامنا} بتقوية قلوبنا، أو باختلاف كلمة الأعداء حتى يتخاذلوا،

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās connects the verse with God forbidding usury while permitting salam, or advance purchase on credit.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: لم حرم الله تعالى الربا أباح السلم فقال:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tadāyun is reciprocal dealing in debt, such as selling to one another on credit; loans are distinct from deferred debts, since classical loans cannot have a term but debts can.
rows.anchor: التداين: تفاعل، من الدين، ومعناه: داين بعضكم بعضا وتبايعتم بدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dāna may mean selling on credit, lending, borrowing, or being heavily indebted; tadayyana and istadāna mean taking debt, illustrated by poetry.
rows.anchor: ويقال من الدين: ادان: إذا باع سلعته (¬1) بثمن إلى أجل

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The exegetes say every right whose due date is deferred is covered by this verse.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون: كل حق مؤجل فهو داخل تحت قوله: {إذا تداينتم بدين}

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī explains the explicit word dayn after tadāyantum by distinguishing financial dealing from moral recompense, since dayn can mean requital too.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الأنباري: إنما ذكر الدين مع أن {تداينتم} يدل عليه؛

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An ajal is the time set for an interval to end; a person’s ajal is death, while a debt’s ajal is its due date, and the root conveys delay.
rows.anchor: معنى الأجل في اللغة: الوقت المضروب لانقضاء الأمد، وأجل الإنسان هو الوقت

rows.speaker: عطاء وابن جريج وإبراهيم وابن جرير
rows.claim: A group, chosen by Ibn Jarīr, treat writing and witnessing deferred debts as obligatory to protect wealth and deter denial; Ibrāhīm says even a tiny handful of greens should be documented.
rows.anchor: وهذا مذهب عطاء (¬2) وابن جريح (¬3) وإبراهيم (¬4) واختيار محمد بن جرير (¬5)

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ regards writing and witnesses as recommendation and permission like the commands in 5:2 and 62:10: documenting is good but leaving it is harmless.
rows.anchor: وقال قوم: هذا أمر ندب وإباحة كقوله: {وإذا حللتم فاصطادوا}

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī agrees that the command is nonbinding because most scholars hold this and obligatory documentation would impose severe hardship; the Prophet described his mission as easy and tolerant.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الأنباري: وهو اختيارنا؛ لاتفاق أكثر العلماء عليه،

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Others say writing, witnesses, or collateral were initially obligatory but were abrogated by the trust clause in 2:283, which permits leaving documentation when the parties trust each other.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون: كانت الكتابة والإشهاد أو الرهن فرضا، ثم نسخ ذلك

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Asked by al-Taymī, al-Ḥasan said the parties may witness or omit witnesses, citing the clause that some may trust others.
rows.anchor: قال التيمي: سألت الحسن عنها فقال: إن شاء أشهد، وإن شاء لم يشهد،

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayd says scholars in the Ḥijāz and Iraq agree that sale witnesses are not mandatory and that buyers can choose; they treat the following trust clause as abrogating the obligation.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيد: والعلماء اليوم من أهل الحجاز وأهل العراق وغيرهم على هذا القول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fair scribe records the debt with equity, granting neither party an advantage, altering neither the amount nor due date, and writing nothing that secretly defeats either party’s right.
rows.anchor: أي: بالحق والإنصاف، لا يكتب لصاحب الدين فضلا على الذي عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A writer must not refuse to document the debt as God taught him; abā means to refuse, and the source also records its use for refusing food.
rows.anchor: أي: لا يمتنع، يقال: أبى فلان الشيء يأباه، إذا امتنع عنه

rows.speaker: مجاهد والربيع
rows.claim: Mujāhid and al-Rabīʿ say the scribe must write when asked because God ordered him not to refuse; al-Farrāʾ says there were few literate people in the Prophet’s time.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد (¬8) والربيع (¬9): واجب على الكاتب أن يكتب إذا أمر

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan limits the duty to cases where no other scribe is available, because refusal would harm the creditor.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: ذاك إذا لم يقدر على كاتب سواه فيضر بصاحب الدين

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says the command initially imposed an obligation on scribe and witness, later abrogated by the ban on harming either one.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك: كانت هذه عزيمة واجبة على الكاتب والشاهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As God taught him may attach to write, meaning write as God commanded, or begin a new clause, meaning write as God favored him with literacy; al-Zajjāj gives both parses.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يتم الكلام عند قوله: {أن يكتب} ثم قال: {كما علمه الله فليكتب}

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses the phrase as what God enabled the person to understand and says one known to write should not refuse the good deed.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: كما أفهمه الله، ولا يمنعن المعروف بكتابة

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says imlāl is the Ḥijāz and Banū Asad form, while imlāʾ is used by Tamīm and Qays; the Qur’an has both forms, as in 25:5.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: أمللت عليه الكتابة لغة الحجاز وبني أسد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The debtor dictates because the debt is being testified against him and his own words reveal what he owes.
rows.anchor: أن (¬4) الذي عليه الدين يملي؛ لأنه المشهود عليه، فيقر على نفسه بلسانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bakhs means diminution; the debtor must acknowledge the amount owed without reducing any part of it.
rows.anchor: البخس: النقصان، يقال: بخسه حقه، إذا نقصه

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid interprets safīh as someone ignorant about dictating the debt.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: جاهلا (¬6) بالإملاء

rows.speaker: الضحاك والسدي
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Suddī interpret safīh as a young child.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك (¬8) والسدي (¬9): طفلا صغيرا

rows.speaker: السدي وابن زيد
rows.claim: Al-Suddī and Ibn Zayd explain weak as incapable or mentally deficient.
rows.anchor: يعني: عاجزا أحمق، عن السدي (¬1) وابن زيد (¬2)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Someone unable to dictate may be mute, impaired, or ignorant of what he owns and owes.
rows.anchor: لخرس أو عي أو (¬3) جهل بما له وعليه

rows.speaker: الضحاك وابن زيد
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Ibn Zayd say the wali is the guardian of a child, incapable person, or fool: a trustee, heir, or other person acting for him.
rows.anchor: قال الضحاك (¬5) وابن زيد (¬6): أي: ولي السفيه والعاجز والطفل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والربيع ومقاتل
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Rabīʿ, and Muqātil instead say the wali is the creditor, who knows the debt best.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس (¬7) والربيع (¬8) ومقاتل (¬9): يعني: ولي الحق، وهو صاحب الدين

rows.speaker: الزجاج وصاحب النظم
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj and the author of al-Naẓm prefer the guardian interpretation: 4:5 calls for guardians to manage dependents’ assets, and taking the creditor as wali would let a claimant’s assertion replace writing and witnesses.
rows.anchor: والقول الأول اختيار الزجاج (¬10) وصاحب النظم، وهو الأظهر والأصح

rows.speaker: صاحب النظم
rows.claim: The passage’s syntax confirms the dependent’s guardian: the debtor is the one who dictates, so his wali must be his representative; a creditor’s representative would have been framed like the earlier scribe.
rows.anchor: وقال صاحب "النظم": الذي يدل عليه نظم هذا الفصل أنه ولي السفيه

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ allows both interpretations of who the wali is.
rows.anchor: وأجاز الفراء القولين جميعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Istashhidū means ashhidū, to call someone as witness; the saying that people testify but are not istushhidūn is explained as saying that they do not testify.
rows.anchor: أي: أشهدوا، يقال: أشهدت الرجل واستشهدته بمعنى (¬7)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two men are free, adult members of the believers’ community, excluding children and enslaved people.
rows.anchor: يعني: من أهل ملتكم من الأحرار البالغين، دون الصبيان والعبيد (¬1)

rows.speaker: الزجاج والفراء وصاحب النظم
rows.claim: The phrase one man and two women can mean the witnesses sought should be one man and two women, let there be that combination, or let that number suffice; each syntactic paraphrase is sound.
rows.anchor: كل هذه التقديرات جائز حسن

rows.speaker: أبو الحسن الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash supplies an implicit kāna; it may take a predicate or be complete, with the complete verb preferred because it requires fewer omitted words, though either reading implies testimony by one man and two women.
rows.anchor: يجوز أن تكون (¬9) (كان) المضمرة في الآية الناصبة للخبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: There is consensus that women’s testimony is admissible in matters of property.
rows.anchor: واجماع أن شهادة النساء جائزة (¬7) في الأموال

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses those whom you approve as people of virtue and religion, like the just witnesses in 65:2; this implies some witnesses should not be accepted.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد: من # أهل الفضل والدين (¬1)، كما في الطلاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source lists ten qualities for an admissible witness: freedom, adulthood, Islam, uprightness, knowledge, no self-serving interest or self-protective motive, no frequent error, no breach of propriety, and no enmity with the party testified against.
rows.anchor: وجملة القول فيمن تقبل شهادته، أن يجتمع فيه عشر خصال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The purpose clause an taḍilla attaches to an implied command to seek one man and two women; it may attach to an implicit verb or to a supplied predicate.
rows.anchor: وذلك أن قوله: {فإن لم يكونا رجلين فرجل وامرأتان} يدل على: فاستشهدوا رجلا وامرأتين،

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وجميع أهل التفسير والمعاني
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and exegetes and language scholars take taḍilla as forget, since the forgetful turns away from recall; 26:20 and al-Farazdaq’s verse illustrate it, while Abū ʿAmr says the root means disappearance.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس (¬1) وجميع أهل التفسير والمعاني: تضل: تنسى،

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī says iḥdā is a feminine form of wāḥid that is used only in an annexed phrase, not by itself.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي: أنثوه على غير بنائه، و (إحدى) لا تستعمل إلا مضمومة إلى غيرها ومضافة،

rows.speaker: أبو العباس عن ابن الأعرابي
rows.claim: Abū al-ʿAbbās transmits Ibn al-Aʿrābī’s forms for pluralizing iḥdā as iḥd, with analogies to kubr/kubrā and poetic attestation.
rows.anchor: وروى أبو العباس عن ابن الأعرابي قال: (¬5) يقال: أحد في جمع إحدى.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An is accusative with a purpose sense: call two women as witnesses so that one can remind the other.
rows.anchor: وموضع (أن) نصب، لأن المعنى: استشهدوا امرأتين، لأن تذكر إحداهما الأخرى،

rows.speaker: سيبويه والبصريون
rows.claim: Sibawayh and the Basran grammarians explain that the verse names forgetting because it causes the needed reminder, as preparing a support because a wall may lean.
rows.anchor: هذا قول سيبويه، وعليه البصريون (¬3).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the clause also says fatudhakkira, the interpretation of an taḍilla as the stated purpose fails: fear of forgetting makes sense, but fear of reminding does not.
rows.anchor: ولما عطف قوله: {فتذكر} على {أن تضل} فسد هذا القول؛

rows.speaker: حمزة
rows.claim: Ḥamza reads in taḍilla with kasra and fatudhakkira in the indicative; inna is conditional, taḍilla is jussive with a joining fatḥa, and the fāʾ introduces the apodosis.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة (إن تضل) بكسر الألف (فتذكر) بالرفع (¬2)،

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: By analogy with 5:95, Sibawayh posits a deleted subject after the apodosis fāʾ, meaning in the matter that one woman reminds the other; the condition and answer modify the indefinite two women.
rows.anchor: وقياس قول سيبويه في قوله: {ومن عاد فينتقم الله منه} [المائدة: 95]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A conditional clause can describe an indefinite noun, as in 22:41; here condition and answer qualify the two women.
rows.anchor: لأن الشرط والجزاء جملة يوصف # بها، كما يوصف (¬1) بها في نحو قوله: {الذين إن مكناهم في الأرض أقاموا الصلاة}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fatudhakkira is read with either gemination or a light consonant; gemination makes dhakara transitive to a second object, supported by 51:55, 88:21 and a poem, while the light form uses hamza-transitivity and omits the object, meaning the testimony.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى {فتذكر} قرئ بالتشديد والتخفيف (¬3) (¬4)،

rows.speaker: عامة المفسرين
rows.claim: Most exegetes understand the other woman to remind her after she forgets.
rows.anchor: وعامة المفسرين على أن هذا التذكير والإذكار من النسيان

rows.speaker: سفيان بن عيينة
rows.claim: Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna instead interprets it as making the other woman a male witness, so their joint testimony counts as a man’s; this is also attributed to Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ and reported through a narration.
rows.anchor: إلا ما يروى عن سفيان بن عيينة أنه قال في قوله: {فتذكر إحداهما الأخرى}

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو بن العلاء
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr distinguishes the readings: geminated means reminding after forgetting; light means one woman reminds the other because the two together stand in a man’s place.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عمرو بن العلا: من قرأ: {فتذكر إحداهما الأخرى} بالتشديد فهو من طريق التذكير

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Exegetes reject the male-equivalence interpretation: women without a man still cannot testify, forgetting should be paired with its opposite, remembering, and equal male status would apply across all legal rulings.
rows.anchor: وأنكر المفسرون هذا التفسير، وضعفوه، من حيث إن النساء لو بلغن ما بلغن

rows.speaker: قتادة والربيع
rows.claim: Qatāda and al-Rabīʿ say the ban on refusing applies when asked to undertake testimony; al-Shaʿbī makes it obligatory only if no one else can do so.
rows.anchor: في قول قتادة (¬4) والربيع (¬5)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس عن عطاء
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, through ʿAṭāʾ, applies it to giving testimony: after entrusting someone with testimony, one may need him to attend court and deliver it.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس، في رواية عطاء: يريد: إذا استودعته الشهادة ثم احتجت إلى شهادة

rows.speaker: مجاهد وعكرمة والسدي وسعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Mujāhid, ʿIkrima, al-Suddī, and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr also understand the verse as testimony’s performance and delivery.
rows.anchor: وهو قول مجاهد (¬2) وعكرمة (¬3) والسدي (¬4) وسعيد بن جبير (¬5)

rows.speaker: الحسن وأبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says the duty covers both undertaking and delivering testimony when the person is available and has no excuse; Abū Isḥāq chooses this view, supported by the adjacent command not to tire of documenting what one witnessed.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول الحسن (¬6) واختيار أبي إسحاق.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saʾāma means weariness or annoyance; the infinitive clause is accusative as the object of that weariness, and the pronouns in write it and its due date refer to the debt.
rows.anchor: والسآمة: الملالة والضجر، يقال: سئمت الشيء أسأمه سأما وسآمة (¬8)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command not to tire of writing is best addressed to creditors: document the rights they lend, small or large, with due date and term; the passage begins by addressing asset and debt holders, while trivial amounts are not normally recorded.
rows.anchor: وأظهر من هذا أن يجعل قوله: {ولا تسأموا أن تكتبوه} خطابا لأولياء الحق،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhālikum refers to the documentation; it is more equitable with God because following God’s command is more just than neglecting it.
rows.anchor: أي: الكتاب {أقسط عند الله} أي: أعدل (¬4)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Written records make testimony more reliable because they remind witnesses, instead of leaving them to impressions; aqwam means more fully upright, and adnā means closer to removing doubt about amount and term.
rows.anchor: {وأقوم للشهادة} لأن الكتاب يذكر الشهود، فتكون شهادتهم (¬2)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A current sale that the parties transact hand to hand can omit documentation because the risks of deferred payment and term are absent.
rows.anchor: فلا جناح في ترك ذلك فيه؛ لأن ما يخاف في النساء والتأجيل يؤمن في البيع يدا بيد (¬5)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here kāna means occur or come into being, as in the usage discussed at 2:280.
rows.anchor: والكون هنا بمعنى: الوقوع والحدوث، كما بينا في قوله: {وإن كان ذو عسرة}

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ allows tadīrūnahā to be accusative as the predicate of kāna; otherwise it is nominative describing a present transaction in circulation.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء (¬6): وان شئت جعلت {تديرونها} في موضع نصب

rows.speaker: عاصم
rows.claim: ʿĀṣim reads tijāratan ḥāḍiratan in the accusative; Abū Isḥāq understands an implied present debt transaction.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عاصم {تجارة حاضرة} بالنصب (¬2)

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī rejects treating tadāyun or the debt in a person’s liability as the name of kāna, since neither is the concrete trade meant here.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي: لا يجوز أن يكون التداين اسم كان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to witness transactions was discussed at the beginning of the verse.
rows.anchor: قد ذكرنا ما في هذا في أول الآية

rows.speaker: طاوس والحسن وقتادة وابن زيد
rows.claim: One reading prohibits harming a scribe or witness through falsifying or altering the record, bearing false testimony, or refusing to testify; the active form has the writer and witness as agents.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول طاوس (¬4) والحسن (¬5) وقتادة (¬6) وابن زيد (¬7)،

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود وعطاء ومجاهد
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd, ʿAṭāʾ, and Mujāhid instead say not to summon a busy scribe or witness when attending would harm him; on this reading the verb is passive.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن مسعود (¬1) وعطاء (¬2) ومجاهد (¬3): معنى الآية: لا يدعى الكاتب وهو مشغول

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj chooses the first interpretation because fisq suits a false witness or person who alters writing, not someone who merely summoned a busy witness; defenders of the second read fisq as sin and disobedience.
rows.anchor: والقول الأول اختيار الزجاج، قال: لقوله: {وإن تفعلوا فإنه فسوق بكم}

rows.speaker: عمر وأبي وابن مسعود ومجاهد
rows.claim: A reading attributed to ʿUmar, Ubayy, Ibn Masʿūd, and Mujāhid vocalizes the verb as passive, supporting the interpretation that a busy witness must not be burdened.
rows.anchor: ويؤكد هذا الثاني: قراءة عمر (¬7) وأبي (¬8) وابن مسعود (¬9) # ومجاهد (¬1)

rows.speaker: أهل اللغة
rows.claim: Language scholars connect safar, travel, with revealing character; related forms include a book that makes things clear, dawn appearing, a woman uncovering her face, reconciling parties by revealing feelings, and sweeping away.
rows.anchor: قال أهل اللغة: سمي السفر سفرا لأنه يسفر عن أخلاق الرجال (¬3)

rows.speaker: ابن الأعرابي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Aʿrābī defines safar as the brightening of dawn; al-Akhṭal’s line describes staying up until the light opens the way.
rows.anchor: ابن الأعرابي: السفر: إسفار الفجر (¬4)

rows.speaker: الأزهري
rows.claim: Al-Azharī explains that a traveler reveals what was hidden by emerging into open country; safar also names the remaining daylight after sunset, illustrated by a weather saying about Sirius.
rows.anchor: وقال الأزهري: وسمي المسافر مسافرا لكشفه قناع الكن عن وجهه،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sāfira and safar are plurals of sāfir, and misfar describes a man strong enough for travel.
rows.anchor: والسافرة والسفر: جمع سافر (¬2)، ورجل مسفر: قوي على السفر (¬3).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rahn is the verbal noun of pledging something with someone; the source cites poetry illustrating the noun and verb.
rows.anchor: الرهن: مصدر رهنت عند الرجل رهنا فأنا أرهنه: إذا وضعته عنده.

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says arhan can mean rahana and cites Ibn Hammām al-Salūlī; al-Aṣmaʿī rejects that reading, preferring arhanahum as a circumstantial clause.
rows.anchor: وأرهنت بمعنى رهنت، لغة عند الفراء، واحتج ببيت ابن همام السلولي:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pledged object is called rahn after a verbal noun shifts into a noun; in this use its case is that of a direct object, not a cognate accusative.
rows.anchor: ولما نقل فسمي به جمع كما تجمع الأسماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As a noun, rahn forms plurals on fuʿul and fiʿāl; the language did not record an afʿul plural, apparently because the frequent plural sufficed.
rows.anchor: فرهن جمع على بناءين من أبنية الجموع وهو فعل وفعال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poetic and lexical evidence supports fuʿul plurals such as ruhun, alongside comparable plural doublets and varied forms quoted from al-Akhfash.
rows.anchor: فرهن: جمع رهن، ثم تخفف العين كما تخفف في رسل وكتب، ونحو ذلك،

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ proposes that ruhan is a plural of rihān, itself a plural of rahn, analogous to thamar as a plural of thimār and jamāʾil from jimāl.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: الرهن: جمع رهان، جمع الجمع،

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr reads ruhun to distinguish pledged collateral from horse-betting: ruhun is common for pledges, while rihān is common for horse races.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عمرو: وإنما قرأت: (فرهن) للفصل بين الرهان في الخيل وبين جمع رهن في غيرها

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj chooses the ruhun reading because it matches the codex and has a sound meaning, following the rule that a reading meeting those conditions is preferred.
rows.anchor: واختار الزجاج هذه القراءة، قال: لأنها موافقة للمصحف،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common rihān reading is the regular plural of rahn, like niʿāl from naʿl; although some allow it as a plural of the plural, the author invokes Sibawayh’s caution against assuming that process without evidence.
rows.anchor: وأما قراءة العامة {فرهان مقبوضة} (¬7) فإنها القياس في جمع رهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rahn derives from something that remains firmly fixed; the cited poetry shows the sense of enduring stability.
rows.anchor: فأما اشتقاق الرهن في اللغة، فأصله: من قولهم: رهن الشيء: إذا دام وثبت،

rows.speaker: اللحياني
rows.claim: Al-Liḥyānī’s forms for trusting someone lead to the verse’s sense: some parties do not fear the other’s betrayal or denial of the debt; the passage cites 8:11 and 12:64.
rows.anchor: قال اللحياني: أمن فلان غيره على الشيء يأمن أمنا وأمنة وأمنة (¬6)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ūtumin is the passive of iftaʿala from amāna; the text gives related active, passive, and participial forms.
rows.anchor: اؤتمن: افتعل، من الأمانة، يقال: أمنته وايتمنته،

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the heart has sinned and acted wickedly when testimony is concealed.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد قد أثم قلبه وفجر (¬3)

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Exegetes note that the threat for concealing testimony specifies sin of the heart; they say it may cause the heart to be transformed into a hypocrite’s heart and sealed.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون: ذكر الله تعالى على كتمان الشهادة نوعا من الوعيد لم يذكره في سائر الكبائر،

rows.speaker: أبو موسى عن النبي
rows.claim: Abū Mūsā reports the Prophet saying that one who conceals testimony when summoned is like one who gave false testimony.
rows.anchor: وروى أبو موسى عن النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم - أنه قال

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan explains ṣbirū as holding to religion and not abandoning it in hardship; al-Zajjāj chooses this interpretation.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن (¬2): اصبروا على دينكم فلا تدعوه لشدة.

rows.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Aslam says the command is to persevere in jihad; Ibn al-Anbārī prefers this view.
rows.anchor: وقال زيد بن أسلم (¬4): أي: على الجهاد.

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ reads ṣbirū as be steadfast with your Prophet and ṣābirū as outlast your enemy so they are never more patient than you.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء (¬6): {اصبروا} مع نبيكم (¬7)، {وصابروا} عدوكم

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says rābiṭū means remain engaged in jihad against the enemy through war and argument; its original association is horses stationed near an enemy frontier.
rows.anchor: قاله الزجاج (¬2). وأصله -عند أهل اللغة-: من (مرابطة الخيل)

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba explains that each side tethered horses at the frontier in readiness, after which remaining at the border was called ribāṭ.
rows.anchor: قال ابن قتيبة (¬4): أصل (المرابطة) و (الرباط): أن يربط هؤلاء خيولهم في الثغر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس عن عطاء
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, through ʿAṭāʾ, interprets the command as standing against God’s and the believers’ enemy until he turns from his religion to theirs; most exegetes see sustained jihad in this command.
rows.anchor: وكلام ابن عباس -في رواية عطاء- يدل على هذه الجملة، فإنه قال في قوله: {ورابطوا}

rows.speaker: أبو سلمة بن عبد الرحمن
rows.claim: Abū Salama ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān says rābiṭū means waiting for one prayer after another; the Prophet’s report from Abū Hurayra calls that ribāṭ three times.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو سلمة بن عبد الرحمن (¬2): معنى {ورابطوا}: انتظروا الصلاة بعد الصلاة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ribāṭ comes from tying or fastening; one who endures something is said to bind his heart or self, so patient persistence in prayer can also be called ribāṭ, as in Labīd’s line.
rows.anchor: وأصل هذا من الربط، وهو: الشد (¬5). ويقال لكل من صبر على أمر

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة وابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda and Ibn al-Anbārī gloss rābiṭū as stand firm and persist; Ibn al-Anbārī cites al-Akhṭal’s ribāṭ as firmness and constancy, linking it to patience and binding oneself.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة (¬2)، وابن الأنباري (¬3): معنى {ورابطوا}؛ أي: اثبتوا، وداوموا
